label: Loving Your Enemies
framing: The command to love your enemies is the hardest thing Jesus ever said, and he meant it without an exit clause. It does not require warm feeling but active goodwill, the refusal to repay evil with evil even when the evil is real and the enemy unrepentant.
cultural: Every culture before Christ and most since have made hating the enemy a virtue, the proof of loyalty to one's own. Even the world of the Old Testament read love your neighbor as license to hate the outsider. Into that universal logic Jesus dropped a command so against the grain that we have spent two thousand years explaining it away, because we still believe, deep down, that our enemies are the exception.
historical: The early Christians stunned the empire by refusing revenge, praying for their persecutors, and dying without cursing, which did more to spread the faith than any argument. Augustine wrestled with how love and justice meet in the use of force, and in the twentieth century figures like Martin Luther King Jr., reading Jesus and Gandhi together, turned enemy-love into a force that broke unjust laws without breaking the law of love.
application: Begin where you can, by praying for the person by name, which is hard to do while plotting against them. Refuse the small revenges, the cold shoulder, the cutting word, the story told to recruit others to your side. Leave the justice to God, who judges rightly, rather than appointing yourself. And remember that you were loved while you were still an enemy of God, which is the only thing that makes this command anything but impossible.

verses.text: You have heard that it was said, ‘Love your neighbor’ and ‘Hate your enemy.’ But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, that you may be sons of your Father in heaven. He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.
verses.where: Jesus quotes the command to love your neighbor together with a line many had added to it, hate your enemy, which the site's note says the law does not contain. He tells his disciples to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them, so that they may be children of the Father who sends sun and rain on the evil and the good. The note says the command is grounded in God's own character.

verses.text: But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return. Then your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High; for He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked. Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.
verses.where: In Luke the command comes with its reason: God is kind to the ungrateful and wicked, and those who act the same way show themselves to be his children. The site's note observes that where Matthew has be perfect, Luke has be merciful. Love for an enemy is not a technique for winning; it is a family likeness.

verses.text: If you encounter your enemy’s stray ox or donkey, you must return it to him. If you see the donkey of one who hates you fallen under its load, do not leave it there; you must help him with it.
verses.where: Among the laws for honest courts, the Book of the Covenant commands Israel to return an enemy's stray ox or donkey and to help the donkey of someone who hates you when it has fallen under its load. The site's note on Matthew 5 points back to this law to show that love for an enemy was already written into Israel's law. It begins with something as ordinary as a neighbor's animal.

verses.text: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.
verses.where: In the collection copied by Hezekiah's scribes, a proverb tells the reader to give food and water to a hungry and thirsty enemy, and promises that the LORD will reward it. The site's note names the command to feed a hungry enemy as one of the chapter's sayings. Paul quotes it in Romans 12, which shows how old the teaching is.

verses.text: And when the king of Israel saw them, he asked Elisha, “My father, shall I kill them? Shall I kill them?” “Do not kill them,” he replied. “Would you kill those you have captured with your own sword or bow? Set food and water before them, that they may eat and drink and then return to their master.” So the king prepared a great feast for them, and after they had finished eating and drinking, he sent them away, and they returned to their master. And the Aramean raiders did not come into the land of Israel again.
verses.where: When an Aramean army sent to seize Elisha is led blinded into Samaria, the king of Israel asks whether he should kill them. Elisha tells him to set food and water before them and send them home. The site's note on the chapter tells how they were fed and sent back, and the passage ends with the raiders no longer coming into Israel's land. Mercy to an enemy here does not mean weakness; it ends a cycle of raids.

verses.text: Jonah, however, was greatly displeased, and he became angry. So he prayed to the LORD, saying, “O LORD, is this not what I said while I was still in my own country? This is why I was so quick to flee toward Tarshish. I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion—One who relents from sending disaster.
verses.where: Jonah is furious that God spared Nineveh, and he finally says why he ran: he knew God was gracious and compassionate and would relent. The site's note on the chapter says God answers by asking whether he should not care about that great city. The story is honest that a prophet can be angry at God's mercy to people he hates, and it leaves the reader with God's question.

verses.text: Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they divided up His garments by casting lots.
verses.where: Jesus' first word from the cross is a prayer for those crucifying him. The site's note says prayer and indifference stand side by side in a single verse, as the soldiers divide his clothes. The plain note says forgiving does not mean saying the wrong was right or staying in danger, and that no one may use his death to justify hatred of any people.

verses.text: While they were stoning him, Stephen appealed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Falling on his knees, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
verses.where: As the stones fall, Stephen kneels and prays that the Lord would not hold this sin against the men killing him. The site's plain note says the first person to die for Jesus dies forgiving, as his Lord did. It adds that the young man holding the coats, Saul, later became the apostle Paul, who wrote that he had been shown mercy.

verses.text: For if, when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life!
verses.where: Paul says that when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son. The site's plain note says the love came first: the cross does not change God's heart toward us, it shows it. It asks the reader what it would mean to make the first move toward peace with an enemy, as God did.

verses.text: Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing.
verses.where: Peter writes to believers suffering for doing right and tells them not to repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing. The site's note on the chapter sets this within his call to unity and compassion. Blessing here is not silence about the wrong; it is a refusal to let the wrong set the terms of the reply.

links.label: Practical guides for life in the world

misread.taken: Love your enemies is used to tell someone who is being hurt that a Christian must feel warmly toward the person hurting them, trust them again, and stay within their reach.
misread.says: The site's plain notes say that loving an enemy does not mean pretending they did no wrong, or trusting someone who is still dangerous. It means wanting their good, praying for them, and refusing to wish them harm. The plain note on Luke 6 adds that turning the other cheek is not a command to stay with someone who is hurting you: Jesus speaks of refusing revenge, not of accepting abuse, and seeking safety and the protection of the law is not disobedience to him.
misread.text: But to those of you who will listen, I say: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.

misread.taken: Heaping burning coals on an enemy's head is sometimes taken as a clever form of revenge: be kind so that they will suffer for it.
misread.says: The site's plain note gives two readings: the coals as the burning shame that undeserved kindness can stir, which may lead an enemy to regret and to make peace, or as a sign that the guilt of one who stays hostile only grows before God. It says the next verse helps: overcome evil with good suggests Paul wants the enemy's good, not his ruin.
misread.text: On the contrary, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink. For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head.”

whole: If the person you are trying to love is hurting you or threatening you now, your safety comes first: tell someone you trust and get help, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Loving an enemy never means staying in their reach. Most people's enemies are not armies. They are an ex-husband, a former friend who spread lies, a boss who tried to ruin them, a relative who will not stop, a neighbor, a person on the other side of a political fight, someone who harmed a child they love. The feeling toward them may be fury, or fear, or a tired bitterness that has settled in for years. And the command of Jesus to love them can sound either impossible or like one more burden laid on the person who was wronged.

Scripture does not pretend enemies are imaginary or that hatred is unnatural. The psalms are full of real enemies. Jonah ran from God because he knew God would be merciful to people he hated, and he said so. Many in Jesus' day had added hate your enemy to the command to love your neighbor, though the law never said it, and the law itself told Israel to return an enemy's stray donkey. The urge to divide the world into those we must love and those we may hate is old and it is in all of us; it shows up in families, churches and nations, on every side. Most of us can name someone we would quietly be glad to see fall. That is not the whole truth about us, but it is part of it, and Jesus speaks to it directly.

So the Bible's wisdom is to love as the Father does, who sends sun and rain on the evil and the good. That love is not first a feeling. It is wanting their good, praying for them by name, refusing to wish them harm, and doing good when an opening comes: food for the hungry enemy, help with the fallen donkey, a blessing instead of an insult. It does not mean pretending the wrong was right; the site's plain note on Jesus' prayer from the cross says ignorance does not make a wrong right. It does not mean trusting someone who is still dangerous, or keeping silent about harm, or dropping a just complaint to the authorities. It means refusing to let the enemy decide who you become. Begin where you can: with a prayer you may not yet mean, as Jesus' own words from the cross can be prayed by someone who does not yet feel them.

The hope Scripture gives is that this love was shown to us first. While we were enemies of God, Paul says, we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son. Jesus prayed for those crucifying him, and Stephen prayed for the men stoning him, and the young man who watched it became the apostle Paul. No one knows what God may do with an enemy, or with us. Elisha's feast ended the raids, and God's mercy to Nineveh angered a prophet who had wanted it destroyed. Love for an enemy will not always be returned in this life. But it is never wasted, because it is the love of the God who will one day set every wrong right, and it makes those who practice it more like their Father.

differ.share: Christians agree that Jesus forbids hatred and personal revenge, that loving an enemy means wanting their good and praying for them, that turn the other cheek is not a command to stay with someone who is hurting you, and that seeking safety and the protection of the law is not disobedience to Jesus.

views.name: No violence at all
views.body: Pacifists, such as the Anabaptists and their heirs the Mennonites, read Jesus' words as forbidding all violence, even in self-defense or war.

views.name: Two kinds of duty
views.body: Martin Luther taught that in your own cause you should bear wrong without revenge, but that a ruler or judge must protect others and punish wrong (Romans 13:4).

views.name: Lawful force to protect the innocent
views.body: The just war tradition, from Augustine to Thomas Aquinas, holds that love of neighbor can require lawful force to protect the innocent, within strict limits.

differ.after: The site's notes on Luke 6 and Matthew 5 set out these readings and do not decide between them. They add that Christians who disagree on war and self-defense agree that these commands condemn hatred.

deep.sit: Who is the one person you would find it hardest to pray for by name, and what is one good thing, safe and wise, you could ask God to do for them?

prayer.lead: An old man's counsel to someone burning over people who have done wrong and seem to prosper. The site's plain note says the psalm does not say it does not matter; it says your anger will not fix it, and God will.
prayer.text: Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him; do not fret when men prosper in their ways, when they carry out wicked schemes. Refrain from anger and abandon wrath; do not fret—it can only bring harm. For the evildoers will be cut off, but those who hope in the LORD will inherit the land.

careLines.text: Seeking safety, and the protection of the law, is not disobedience to Jesus.
If you are being harmed, tell someone you trust and get help.
Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
